draft.title: Budget outcomes
card: A budget outcome compares what the government raises in revenue with what it spends in a year. There are three outcomes.
spending is greater than revenue. Surplus: revenue is greater than spending.

The usual measure is the underlying cash balance, which is revenue minus spending in cash terms. It is often shown as a share of GDP, so the size of the budget can be compared with the size of the economy.
draft.remember: Revenue minus spending gives the outcome: below zero is a deficit, above zero is a surplus.

a.q: In one year, a government raises $480 billion in revenue and spends $500 billion. What is the budget outcome?
opts: A deficit of $20 billion
A surplus of $20 billion
A balanced budget
A deficit of $980 billion
a.why: Spending is greater than revenue, so the outcome is a deficit. The gap is $500 billion minus $480 billion, which is $20 billion. A surplus would need revenue to be the larger figure.
a.clue: Which is larger, revenue or spending?

b.q: A budget shows an underlying cash balance of -1.5% of GDP. What does this tell us?
opts: Spending was greater than revenue, equal to 1.5% of GDP
Revenue was greater than spending, equal to 1.5% of GDP
Revenue equalled spending, so the budget was balanced
Spending was 1.5% of GDP, and revenue was zero
b.why: A negative cash balance means revenue minus spending is below zero, so the budget is in deficit. The gap is measured as a share of GDP. The minus sign does not mean a surplus.
b.clue: A negative result for revenue minus spending means what?

b.best: Spending was greater than revenue, equal to 1.5% of GDP

problems.detail: "So the size of the budget can be compared with the size of the economy" is loose. Showing the cash balance as a share of GDP compares the size of the deficit or surplus with the economy, not the size of the whole budget. A student could read it as total spending relative to GDP. Suggest "so the size of the deficit or surplus can be compared with the size of the economy."

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are correct, each with one right answer. One minor wording fix on the card: the share of GDP compares the deficit or surplus with the economy, not the size of the whole budget.
